'''''Sadleria cyatheoides''''', commonly known as '''{{okina}}ama{{okina}}uma{{okina}}u fern'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SACY3|taxon=Sadleria cyatheoides|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> or '''{{okina}}ama{{okina}}u''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Chock |first=Alvin K. |date=1968 |title=Hawaiian Ethnobotanical Studies I. Native Food and Beverage Plants |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4252960 |journal=Economic Botany |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=221–238 |doi=10.1007/BF02861956 |jstor=4252960 |bibcode=1968EcBot..22..221C |issn=0013-0001|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is a [[fern]] species in the family [[Blechnaceae]].

== Description ==
Reaching a height of {{convert|0.9|-|1.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} and a trunk diameter of {{convert|7.5|-|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}}, {{okina}}ama{{okina}}u resembles a small [[Cyatheales|tree fern]].

The young fronds are often tinged red to block harmful sunlight.<ref name="HVNP">Read on a sign in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park on 31.10.2013</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is [[Endemism|endemic]] to [[Hawaii]] and inhabits [[lava]] flows, open areas, and [[Hawaiian tropical rainforests#Wet forests|wet forests]] on all major [[Hawaiian Islands|islands]] up to an altitude of {{convert|1676|m|ft|abbr=on}}.

== Uses ==
Its pith and young fronds are edible either [[Kālua|roasted]] or steamed.<ref name=":0" />

== In culture ==
[[Kīlauea]]'s [[Halemaʻumaʻu]] is named for this species.<ref name="CFTH">{{cite web |last=Little Jr. |first=Elbert L. |author2=Roger G. Skolmen |year=1989 |title=ʻAmaʻu, sadleria |url=http://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/forestry/trees/CommonTreesHI/CFT_Sadleria_cyatheoides.pdf |accessdate=2011-06-14 |work=Common Forest Trees of Hawaii (Native and Introduced) |publisher=United States Forest Service}}</ref>
